extracted.intended_audience: credit card issuers, industry trade associations, consumer groups, lawyers, academics, and other stakeholders participating in CFPB rulemaking on late fees (Regulation Z)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and final rulemaking rationale for amending Regulation Z (TILA) provisions governing credit card late fees, including safe harbor thresholds, cost-analysis methodology, data sources, and considerations specific to larger vs smaller card issuers. Includes descriptions of the CFPB's data, analytical methods, statutory interpretation, and responses to public comments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reasonable and proportional standard (TILA §149)
rubrics_metrics.description: The amount of any penalty fee (including late fees) must be “reasonable and proportional” to the omission or violation under TILA section 149.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In evaluating reasonableness and proportionality, the CFPB was guided by four statutory factors used in the Board's 2010 Final Rule: (1) cost incurred by the creditor from an omission or violation; (2) deterrence of omissions or violations by the cardholder; (3) the conduct of the cardholder; and (4) such other factors deemed necessary or appropriate. The CFPB used these principles in assessing safe harbor thresholds and the appropriateness of cost-analysis approaches.

rubrics_metrics.name: Safe harbor provisions (§1026.52(b)(1)(ii))
rubrics_metrics.description: Optional safe harbor amounts that, if adhered to by issuers, are presumed to be reasonable and proportional penalty fees under TILA.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The CFPB proposed and ultimately establishes changes for Larger Card Issuers: repeal the current safe harbor thresholds and establish a new safe harbor of $8 for late fees charged by Larger Card Issuers. The proposal considered (and solicited comment on) eliminating safe harbors entirely (for late fees or all penalty fees), lowering the safe harbor to $8, eliminating higher safe harbor amounts for subsequent violations, and removing CPI annual adjustments for the safe harbor amount. The safe harbor is an alternative to the cost-analysis method in §1026.52(b)(1)(i).

rubrics_metrics.name: Cost-analysis provisions for determining penalty fees (§1026.52(b)(1)(i))
rubrics_metrics.description: An alternative to safe harbor: issuers may determine penalty fee amounts by conducting a cost analysis to show amounts are reasonable and proportional.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The CFPB (and the Board's 2010 rule) limit collection costs in the cost analysis to pre-charge-off collection costs. If safe harbors are eliminated, issuers would need to use the cost analysis provisions (subject to limitations in §1026.52(b)(2)). The CFPB considered whether cost analysis provisions would need amendment if safe harbors were eliminated.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limit late-fee amount as share of required payment (proposed 25% cap)
rubrics_metrics.description: Proposed amendment that late fee amounts must not exceed 25 percent of the required payment; currently late fees may not exceed 100 percent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The 2023 Proposal would amend §1026.52(b)(2)(i)(A) to provide the 25 percent cap. The CFPB solicited comments on this change and used examples and commentary edits to align examples with a proposed $8 safe harbor.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exclude post-charge-off collection costs from cost calculations
rubrics_metrics.description: Costs for purposes of cost-analysis provisions do not include collection costs incurred after an account is charged off pursuant to loan loss provisions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consistent with the Board's 2010 Final Rule, the CFPB did not propose to change this limitation and limited its safe-harbor calculation to pre-charge-off costs by estimating and excluding post-charge-off collection costs (notably commissions paid to third-party debt collectors). CFPB estimated pre-charge-off collection costs to be approximately 75 percent of Y-14 reported collection costs based on observed post-charge-off commission ratios (around 25 percent).

rubrics_metrics.name: Treatment of subsequent late fees within same/next six billing cycles
rubrics_metrics.description: The existing rule had provided a higher safe harbor dollar amount for subsequent violations of the same type that occur during the same billing cycle or in one of the next six billing cycles; the proposal would remove that higher safe harbor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The 2023 Proposal would amend §1026.52(b)(1)(ii) to no longer apply a higher safe harbor dollar amount for subsequent late fees in the same billing cycle or within the next six billing cycles; examples and commentary were proposed to be revised accordingly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Annual CPI adjustments to safe harbor amounts
rubrics_metrics.description: Current provision allows annual adjustments to safe harbor dollar amounts to reflect changes in the CPI.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The proposal would provide that CPI annual adjustments would not apply to the late-fee safe harbor amount (i.e., remove CPI indexing for late-fee safe harbor). CFPB solicited comment on this change.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conditional requirements for using safe harbor (automatic payments / notifications)
rubrics_metrics.description: Solicited comment on whether as a condition of using the safe harbor, issuers should be required to offer automatic payment options or provide notification of the payment due date within a certain number of days prior to the due date, or both.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is a proposed conditionality the CFPB sought input on; it would link availability of the safe harbor to issuer practices that reduce the likelihood of late payments (e.g., autopay for minimum payment, pre-due-date notices).

rubrics_metrics.name: Prohibition on charging late fees for payments within 15 days after due date (solicited)
rubrics_metrics.description: The CFPB solicited comment on whether card issuers should be prohibited from imposing late fees on consumers that make the required payment within 15 calendar days following the due date.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This was a question posed in the proposal for public comment; no mandatory rule text is specified here but CFPB sought feedback on feasibility and effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Data sources and required metrics for analysis
rubrics_metrics.description: Four primary data sources considered: (1) Y-14; (2) Y-14+; (3) credit card debt collection data from an information order under section 1022(c)(4) of the CFPA; and (4) the CFPB's Credit Card Agreement Database. The Y-14 data provided metrics: Late Fee Income, Collection Costs, Late Fee Amount, Total Required Payments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: CFPB described each source, why it relied on them, confidentiality constraints (Y-14 contains confidential supervisory information), and the specific definitions used (e.g., Late Fee Income = reported net fee income assessed for late or nonpayment accounts). The CFPB provided aggregated summaries (Revenue-Costs Report) where raw Y-14 data could not be released.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of Y-14 data: coverage, sampling, and confidentiality
rubrics_metrics.description: Y-14 data are collected from large bank holding companies and contain confidential supervisory information; Y-14 issuers in CFPB analysis account for just under 70 percent of outstanding U.S. consumer credit card balances as of year-end 2020. CFPB used complete portfolio data and a random 40 percent subsample of account information for certain analyses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: CFPB explained limitations on releasing raw data but provided aggregated/anonymized values and detailed methodological descriptions so commenters could meaningfully comment; used random 40% subsample for account-level analyses and required existence of all four metrics for inclusion in sample.

rubrics_metrics.name: Methodology to estimate pre-charge-off vs post-charge-off collection costs
rubrics_metrics.description: Because Y-14 reports total collection costs, CFPB estimated the portion that is post-charge-off (primarily commissions paid to third-party debt collectors) and excluded post-charge-off costs to derive pre-charge-off collection costs for cost analysis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: CFPB examined confidential data on commissions paid by six major issuers (representing 91% of balances among portfolios with positive collection expenses) to estimate post-charge-off commission shares; used recovery and commission rates to calculate estimated post-charge-off commission costs and divided by total collection costs to estimate the share. Based on this, CFPB estimated post-charge-off costs ~25% and pre-charge-off ~75% of reported collection costs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Revenue-to-cost ratio calculation (late fee income to estimated pre-charge-off collection costs)
rubrics_metrics.description: CFPB compared each month's late-fee income for a portfolio to the portfolio's average estimated pre-charge-off collection costs for that month to produce monthly estimates of the late-fee-income-to-cost ratio (from 2013 to early 2022).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This methodology used estimated pre-charge-off costs that occur two through six months later; CFPB generated monthly estimates and used them in assessing whether proposed safe-harbor amounts recover collection costs and in forming policy conclusions. CFPB published a Revenue-Costs Report with aggregated monthly values to aid commenters.

rubrics_metrics.name: Y-14+ and Credit Card Agreement Database use for issuer-size inference
rubrics_metrics.description: Y-14+ includes additional specialized issuers and was used to calculate average late fees for those issuers; the Credit Card Agreement Database provided information on maximum late fee amounts across many issuers (including smaller ones).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: CFPB used Y-14+ average late fee (e.g., $31 in 2019 and 2020) and agreement database review (over 500 issuers) to infer that smaller issuers generally charged lower late fees than the largest issuers; these data influenced consideration of impacts on smaller issuers and whether to apply $8 threshold to them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consideration of small issuers and SBREFA concerns
rubrics_metrics.description: Industry commenters and the SBA Office of Advocacy raised concerns that the proposed $8 safe harbor and use of Y-14 data (from large issuers) may not accurately represent collection costs of smaller issuers and could impose undue burdens, triggering SBREFA considerations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: CFPB acknowledged concerns and considered whether to develop separate safe harbor amounts or ensure cost-analysis alternatives would not unduly burden small issuers. The CFPB did not, at this time, impose the new $8 threshold on Smaller Card Issuers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Statistical analysis approaches for behavioral effects (seventh-month analysis)
rubrics_metrics.description: CFPB conducted a seventh-month analysis on a random subsample of account-level Y-14 data to investigate whether lower late fees in month seven lead to a discontinuous jump in late payments in the seventh month after the last late payment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: CFPB described the statistical approach and methodologies used and disclosed that an academic commenter requested release of the underlying Y-14 data for replication; CFPB argued the Proposal provided sufficient methodological description and aggregated data (Revenue-Costs Report) for commenters to evaluate the analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transparency and disclosure standard in rulemaking using confidential supervisory data
rubrics_metrics.description: When relying on confidential supervisory (Y-14) or information-order data, the agency must disclose sufficient information (source, methodology, number of accounts, characteristics, aggregate results) to allow meaningful comment even if raw data cannot be published.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: CFPB defended its use of confidential data, noting legal protections (Board instructions, FOIA exemptions, 12 CFR 1070.40-.48) and pointed to the Proposal and Revenue-Costs Report as providing detailed descriptions of data sources, metrics, methodology, and aggregate findings so commenters could meaningfully evaluate the rulemaking.

rubrics_metrics.name: Effective date timing of final rule
rubrics_metrics.description: The CFPB generally proposed that the final rule, if adopted, would take effect 60 days after publication in the Federal Register.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This was the proposed implementation timetable described in the 2023 Proposal.
